text.p: The following are the main stories from Friday morning's German newspapers:
FRANKFURTER ALLGEMEINE ZEITUNG
- Parliament agrees amendment to federal nature protection law, a compromise between conservationists and users of nature.
- Ruling coalition divided over proposed change to citizenship law.
- Frankfurt mayor Petra Roth elected to postion of president of parliament of German cities.
- Spending freeze announced by Finance Minister Theo Waigel will only save around two billion marks.
- Economic recovery stays subdued in first quarter, according to latest government statistics, with growth up just 0.5 percent on the same period last year for the quarter.
HANDELSBLATT
- German economy slowly starts to pick up -- up an annual 1.4 percent based on first quarter figures. Exports remain main engine of growth in both Germany and France.
- Bernhard Jagoda, President of the Federal Labour Office, expects an average of 4.2 million unemployed in Germany this year.
- Agreement in sight between Finance Minister Theo Waigel and city governments ober planned reduction to corporate taxes.
- Head of Germany's largest union IG Metall Klaus Zwickel sticks to view that length of working week should be cut.
- German prosecutors probe Daimler-Benz senior executive over allegations of passing on insider information.
SUEDDEUTSCHE ZEITUNG
- Members of Finance Minister Theo Waigel's Christian Social Union (CSU) discussing a possible delay in the start of Europe's single currency due to the left-wing victory in French elections.
- German health insurers out of pocket by 2.5 billion marks in first quarter of 1997 despite stagnating payouts.
- German public television network ARD will be one billion marks short until 2000.
- Parliament votes in favour of reworked controversial nature protection law.
DIE WELT
- Five former German soldiers jailed for clubbing two Turks with baseball bats and threatening an Italian with a knife in March in a racist attack.
- Parliament votes in favour of new nature protection law.
- Waigel urges junior coalition partners the Free Democrats (FDP) to cooperate on the financing of the 1998 budget.
